sentences.text: The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — of Gnatusuchus is a nearly complete skull (MUSM 990) found in the Iquitos area of Peru, accompanied by three partial mandible specimens.
Gnatusuchus had highly reduced dentition with only 14 upper teeth and 11 lower teeth, far fewer than the 18 to 20 found in other blunt-snouted caimans.
The front teeth of Gnatusuchus were long, peg-like, and procumbent, showing signs of wear on their tips.
The rear teeth of Gnatusuchus were globular in shape with a distinct neck.
Based on skull measurements, researchers estimate Gnatusuchus reached a total body length between 148.9 and 167.7 centimeters.
The genus name Gnatusuchus combines the Quechua word for 'small nose' and the Greek word for 'crocodile'.
The genus name comes from the Quechua word ñatu, meaning 'small-nosed', while the species name refers to the Amazonian city of Pebas.
Researchers hypothesize that Gnatusuchus used its front teeth to shovel food while crushing bivalve shells with its tightly packed rear teeth.
Gnatusuchus pebasensis was named in 2015 based on a nearly complete skull and several jaws found in the Pebas Formation near Iquitos in Peru.
The youngest fossil records of Gnatusuchus come from the Nueva Unión area south of Iquitos, Peru.
Gnatusuchus lived alongside six other crocodilian species, including two other caimans with crushing dentitions: Kuttanacaiman iquitosensis and Caiman wannlangstoni.
Research suggests that specialized crushing dentition was an ancestral trait in Caimaninae, as basal members like Kuttanacaiman and Globidentosuchus also possessed this feature.
Gnatusuchus is classified within the family Alligatoridae.
Gnatusuchus belongs to the subfamily Caimaninae.
Gnatusuchus belongs to the parent group Caimaninae.
Gnatusuchus is a member of the class Reptilia.
The type species of the genus Gnatusuchus is Gnatusuchus pebasensis.
Phylogenetic analysis places Gnatusuchus as the most basal member of the Caimaninae subfamily.
A phylogenetic analysis published with its original scientific description places Gnatusuchus as the most basal member of the Caimaninae clade.
Gnatusuchus lived during the Langhian to Serravallian stages, from 15.98 to 11.63 million years ago.
Gnatusuchus lived approximately 13 million years ago in the Pebas mega-wetlands, a vast system covering over one million square kilometers in modern-day Peru.
It is noted that Gnatusuchus has not been found in the Urumaco or Solimões formations where other durophagous caimans persisted after the Pebas wetlands declined.
It is debated whether the re-emergence of crushing dentition in derived species like Caiman wannlangstoni represents a convergent evolution rather than a retention of the ancestral trait.
